title: REDACTED — a roguelike deckbuilder where you run an illegal printing press and the "cards" are movable type
author: strugglingwordsmith
selftext:
Quick origin story, because people always ask: I play Balatro, Slay the Spire 2 and Dice a Million, and I built this with Claude Code. Not "generate me a game" — I asked for \*\*playable prototypes instead of design docs\*\*, and by the end of the first session I had two single-file HTML games I could actually click on. I picked the printing press one, and then spent days as the world's most annoying playtester, asking for things in roughly this order: make it intuitive (a live pattern chart, Balatro-style stage-then-print controls), then \*deeper\* (an economy, districts, boss censors, characters, a difficulty ladder), then \*tenser\*, then \*pretty\*. The one decision I didn't make and would never have made myself: it structured the prototype so every number and every word of content lived in a single data block, with the mechanics code below holding no literals of its own. At the time that felt like over-engineering a toy. It's the whole reason porting the finished thing to Godot 4 took days instead of weeks — the content moved across verbatim, hash-checked, and only about six functions had to be rewritten.

The most useful thing it ever did, though, was write two bots to play the game for me: an "optimal" one that brute-forces every legal play in your hand, and a "casual" one that grabs four tiles sharing a first letter, never touches a banned word, and never uses its ability. That turned every balance argument from "this feels hard" into "the casual bot dies on night 6, which is exactly where it's supposed to die," and every change since has been A/B'd over 120 runs with the new layer switched on and off. It caught things playtesting never would have. A character I'd given heat immunity to scored \*\*88,000 against a 2,600 quota\*\*. A boss meant to punish long words was quietly deleting an entire character, until we halved their score instead of zeroing it. A multiplier cap of ×8 instead of ×10 was a 66% loss rate for one printer. And when one character felt miserable at high difficulty, the obvious culprit — a nightly pay cut — turned out to recover nothing when we dropped modifiers one at a time on identical seeds; the real killer was a +1 shop markup pricing that character out of the one bribe it depends on. Win rate 45% → 70%.



Two more things worth saying, because the pitch usually skips them. It found bugs by \*measuring\* rather than reading: the best one was a hard freeze on night 6 — every single run, guaranteed — caused by a UI trim loop counting child nodes that had been queued for deletion but hadn't been freed yet, so the loop could never exit. A headless test found it in about a minute. And it repeatedly caught its own earlier numbers being wrong and wrote that down rather than quietly tuning toward them: at one point every win rate in the project was measuring "cleared night 7" while claiming to measure night 9, which meant a character I thought won 88% of the time actually won 45%. That's a number I'd have shipped on. My contribution through all of it was mostly taste and stubbornness — pick the theme, kill the bad ideas, say when the trailer voice-over sounded too robotic, and always ask for the measurement instead of the opinion.



So, the game



You have a cellar, a press, and a case of movable type. The Ministry keeps a list of what the city is allowed to read, and you are not on it.



Every night you set words into the press bed and pull a print. Lines score as chips × mult through \*\*rhetoric patterns\*\* — alliteration, rhyme, crescendo, echo, doublet, manifesto — so it plays like a poker hand you compose out of vocabulary instead of one you're dealt.



Then there's the gamble. \*\*Banned words double your line.\*\* Two of them quadruple it. They also stack Heat superlinearly, and at 100 Heat somebody kicks the door in, takes two of your tiles and half your money. The whole game is that dial.



\*\*What's in it:\*\*



\- \*\*Nine nights, three districts.\*\* A \*\*Censor\*\* arrives on every third one, and each breaks something different you'd come to rely on — one redacts a tile from your hand every print, one kills alliteration \*and\* rhyme outright, one caps your multiplier, one seals your five longest words before the night even starts. The shop warns you which is coming the night before, so a censor is a puzzle you get to prepare for, not a wall you walk into.

\- \*\*Fonts are your jokers.\*\* 25 of them, and the good ones are opinions rather than stat lines: one feeds on the Heat it generates, one pays you for \*restraint\*, one turns every line into money.

\- \*\*Type wears out.\*\* Every slug you print chips and eventually breaks. Your deck is a physical object that degrades.

\- \*\*A night market with five vendors\*\*, each with their own stock and prices. The Fence sells contraband under cost and raises the Heat every time. The Widow's bulk type arrives half worn already. Every night has one genuine bargain and one item priced for fools.

\- \*\*Sorts and Proofs.\*\* Sorts are qualities you file into type you already own — a slug that rhymes on its \*first\* letter, a ligature that counts as two words, a filing that makes a clean word count as contraband. Proofs are one-use favours you spend \*mid-night\*, including a watchman who looks the other way for exactly one line.

\- \*\*Three printers.\*\* The Poet rhymes, the Agitator burns the evidence, the Archivist never runs short. Each has a censor that is specifically their nemesis.

\- \*\*Getting out is its own scene.\*\* Meet the final quota and you still have to leave the city, carrying whatever Heat you earned getting there. Front gate, harbour or rooftops — and getting caught means you were a martyr, which is a lovely thing to be and a terrible thing to unlock nothing with.

\- \*\*Four Crackdown levels\*\* above the standard run, unlocked per character, and an endless city for anyone who escapes.



Made in Godot 4. The soundtrack is generated live and wired to your Heat — the filter opens and the notes crowd in as the night gets worse, and a heartbeat starts on censor nights.



[https://seesawc23.itch.io/redacted](https://seesawc23.itch.io/redacted)



\*Print what they told you not to.\*
